answers.mern_react_exp_l1_01: I built a job search filter component in my final year project. It let users narrow results by skill and location. The hardest part was keeping filters in sync with the URL, so I stored the filter state in one place and then read it from the query string.
answers.mern_react_con_l1_01: Props are passed down from the parent and are read-only, whereas state is owned by the component and can change. When state changes, React re-renders the component, which is why a counter updates on screen.
answers.mern_react_con_l2_01: useEffect runs side effects after the component renders. The dependency array controls when it runs again: an empty array runs it once, and if a value in the array changes it runs again. A cleanup function runs before the next run, so for example a timer or subscription does not leak.
answers.mern_react_scn_l2_01: First I would disable the submit button while the request is in flight and track a loading state, because that stops the second click. However the user could still refresh, so I would also make the server endpoint safe to repeat with an idempotency key.
answers.mern_react_scn_l3_01: I would open the React Profiler first to find which component renders most, because guessing wastes time. Then I would memoize the expensive ones with React.memo or useMemo, keep state local so a change does not re-render the whole page, and virtualize long lists. In my project this cut a 400 item list render from about 1 second to 200 ms.
answers.mern_node_scn_l3_01: At 10,000 requests per minute I would keep the services stateless behind a load balancer so I can add instances. Caching handles read-heavy endpoints, database indexes keep queries fast, and rate limiting protects the API. The first bottleneck is usually the database, so I would watch query times and add read replicas if needed.
